title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `k`, reverse the nodes of the list `k` at a time, and return the resulting list. If the number of nodes remaining at the end is not a multiple of `k`, leave that final group of nodes as-is (in original order). You must only rearrange nodes by manipulating pointers — you may not change the values stored in the nodes.

The list is given as an array (e.g. `[1,2,3,4,5]` represents `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null`). The starter code includes helpers to convert between the array and a linked-list node — build the actual list, reverse it group by group, then convert back to an array to return.

examples.explanation: Groups of 2 are reversed: (1,2)->(2,1), (3,4)->(4,3); the leftover single node 5 stays as-is.
The first group of 3 is reversed; only 2 nodes remain after that, fewer than k, so they stay in original order.
With k = 1 (the minimum allowed), every 'group' has exactly one node, so reversing each group changes nothing.

constraints: The number of nodes is n
hints: First check whether at least k nodes remain from the current position — if not, that final partial group must be left untouched.
If a full group of k nodes exists, reverse just those k nodes using the standard iterative reversal (three pointers: prev, curr, next), stopping after exactly k steps.

After reversing a group, the ORIGINAL first node of that group is now its tail, and its next pointer needs to be connected to the (recursively or iteratively processed) result of reversing the rest of the list from where the group ended — and the node before this group needs to point to the group's new head.

solution.approach: Use a dummy node before head, with `group_prev` tracking the node just before each group. For each group, first walk k steps ahead to confirm k nodes actually remain; if not, stop entirely (the remainder is left as-is). If a full group exists, reverse those k nodes in place with the standard three-pointer iterative reversal. The original first node of the group becomes its new tail, so its next is connected to whatever comes after the group (found before reversing), and group_prev.next is pointed at the group's new head (the former last node). Advance group_prev to the original first node (now the group's tail) and repeat for the next group.
